It, as he did David, Job xxxiv. 30., and Daniel ii. 20. (Calmet)
The scribe. That is, the man that is wise and learned in the law. (Challoner) — It also denotes an officer, Judges v. 14. God must give light and success. (Calmet)

Injury, out of revenge. (Haydock) (Leviticus xix. 18.) — “Cæsar used to forget nothing but injuries.” (Cicero, Ligar.) — This at least is the character of a great man. (St. Augustine, ep. 138., and 54.)

Men. It invades the rights of the former, and disturbs the repose of mankind. — All. Greek is obscure, “and from both proceeds injustice;” (Calmet) or, “it shall act unjustly.” (Haydock) — Pride attacks both God and man. (Grotius)
Deceits. Hence kingdoms are changed. (Worthington) — The ambition and luxury of subjects (Cato) and the negligence of the rulers, bring on confusion. (St. Augustine, City of God v. 13.)
Man. The desire of plunder, or of glory, occasions revolutions. (Haydock) — Covetousness is the root of all evils, and causes people to abandon the faith, 1 Timothy vi. 10. (Worthington)
Bowels, and would have no compassion for others or for himself. Some Greek copies leave out as far as sale, but Grabe replaces the omission from the Complutensian.

Beginning, or summit; arche. (Calmet) — Thus Lucifer and Adam fell by pride. (St. Augustine, City of God xii. 6.) All sin, being a contempt of God, springs from pride, (Prosper. contemp. iii. 3.) and from an inordinate self-love. (Calmet)
Sin, because man abandons God’s law, and falls into all misery. (Worthington) — The proud easily yield to all sorts of iniquity. (Menochius)
Disgraced. Greek, “hath taken an exemplary vengeance, and hath,” &c. (Haydock) — Them, as he did the giants, Sodom, Nabuchodonosor, &c.
Stead. Luke i. 52. (Calmet) — “Thales being asked what was difficult to be seen; replied, a tyrant grown old.” (Laertius 1.)
Nations, the Chanaanites, who submitted to the yoke: or rather the Hebrews. (Calmet) — Greek, “instead of them.”
Foundation: overturning Sodom, Babylon, and even Jerusalem, for their sins. (Calmet)

Wise. When Diogenes was exposed to sale, and asked what he could do, he answered, “I know how to command free men.” (Laertius 6.) — Joseph and Daniel obtained authority by their wise conduct. (Calmet)
Desert. Let not avarice deprive thee of the necessities of life, nor do any thing beneath thy dignity, Luke xxi. 19.
Glorified. Greek, “honoured on account of his knowledge, and the rich is, ” &c. (Haydock)
And. Greek omits this sentence: (Calmet) yet Grabe has, And the man who is without honour in wealth, how much more so will he be in poverty? (Haydock) (Ecclesiastes vii. 12.)

Men. Merit is preferable to high birth, as it surmounts difficulties. (Calmet) — Those who humble themselves, like Daniel, or fall under the oppression of others unjustly, as Joseph did, shall be exalted by God. (Worthington)
Look. “The most robust is farthest removed from wisdom.” (Cicero) — The beauty of the soul must be regarded. (St. Ambrose, Virg. 3.) (Calmet)
Sweetness. Honey was more esteemed before sugar became common. As the little bee produces such sweetness, so the less beautiful often by their abilities surpass the comely.

Throne. Greek, “pavement.” Dionysius II, tyrant of Syracuse, was forced to turn schoolmaster at Corinth. (Calmet) — Crown. Abdalonymus, a gardener, was placed on the throne of Sidon; (Curt. 4.) and several Roman emperors had been of the meanest condition. (Pliny, [Natural History?] xxxv. 18.) David was a shepherd.

Man, as David did Miphiboset, 2 Kings xvi. 4. Constantine the Great grieved for having put his son Crispus to death on too weak evidence; and Theodosius repented for the sentence he had rashly passed on the inhabitants of Thessalonica. Even though the sentence should happen to be just, it would be wrong to pronounce it too hastily.
Discourse. This is a mark of impertinence, Proverbs xviii. 13. (Calmet) — Let others finish their sentence, and wait if there be any elder or better informed to speak. (Worthington)
Escape. God will grant thee riches without so much solicitude (Lyranus) or rather meddle not with too many things, as that is the way to succeed in none, and destroys all repose.

Sinners. They are all born in sin. But some appear to have worse dispositions than others, Psalm lvii. 4. (Calmet) — God is not the author of iniquity. (Haydock) — He punishes in order to save, though he be offended by the wicked choice of man. (Calmet) — Blindness of heart and obduracy are punishments of sin. (Worthington)
Ever. All things work together for the good of the elect, Romans viii. 8. (Haydock) — God never abandons first. (Council of Trent, Session vii. 11.) — The wicked often abuse graces. (Calmet)
Covenant. All the Israelites partook in the covenants entered into between God and their fathers, which became their own by circumcision, as we become entitled to the alliance of Christ by baptism.
Place. If God bestow not riches, it may be for thy advantage.
Fruit. Prosperity was a sign of God’s favour, under the old law. Now nothing is more equivocal, and the poor are declared blessed. (Calmet)

Myself. Neither the poor nor the rich can be independent of God. (Haydock) — Perhaps no one dares to hold this language. But many act as if they thought themselves gods, and some have claimed divine honours, 4 Kings xviii. 34., Isaias xiv. 13., and Ezechiel xxix. 3.

Death, in old age, (Grotius) or rather after the soul’s departure. The pagans had not this consolation. Their hopes were confined to the earth; and as they saw many honest people miserable, they introduced a chimerical idea of happiness, consisting in virtue alone. The views of Christians are chiefly bent on future rewards.
Hour. The last of life. It demonstrates the vanity of past pleasures. Even a momentary toothache will banish the recollection of such delights.

Children. If they take wicked ways, it is a stain on their father’s memory; and though the latter were blameless, it must greatly disturb their repose. (Calmet) — Children may here denote the works of man, which can only then be pronounced perfect, when he is incapable of falling from the state of virtue. (Haydock)
Own. So Herod destroyed his wife’s family, and Paris stole Helen. (Calmet)

To whom. All must not be admitted into the house, nor treated with marks of particular esteem. Yet daily alms must be given without too scrupulous an enquiry, Luke vi. 30. (Calmet) — It would be wrong to encourage sinners, who would run to their ruin. But we must relieve the penitent. (Worthington)
Lord. Christ rewards what good is done to his poor brethren.

For. Greek, (4.) “Give to the pious, and receive not the sinner, (6.) Do,” &c. (Haydock) — The gospel enjoins us to do good to all. St. Augustine (Dort. iii. 16.) and St. Thomas Aquinas (ii. 2. q. xxxii. a ix.) explain this in a spiritual sense, that we must not partake in the crimes of others. We may also make presents to the virtuous, and pass over people of a different character, particularly when they would abuse our gifts. The honest poor must be preserved.

Rusteth. So his malice always returns, (Calmet) and he shews what he is. (Vatable) — Christianity does not blame due reserve in treating with those whom we know not, or who have formerly injured us. Though we must love them from our heart, yet we need not intrust our secrets to them, nor even to every friend. Joab always retained a hatred for Abner, and Absalom for his brother and father, though they dissembled their resentment. (Calmet) — So the wicked commonly act. (Haydock) — We must love, but not trust them, being wise as serpents, Matthew x. (Worthington)

Of him. Greek adds, “and thou shalt be to him as one who has rubbed a mirror, (of brass from the rust. It returns perpetually. Calmet) and shalt know that the rust is not removed for ever. (Grabe) (Haydock)

Beasts. Vipers, &c. Why should they familiarize themselves with such? Some Italians still handle serpents without fear, pretending that they are the descendants of St. Paul. (Calmet) — But he was never married, (1 Corinthians vii.; Haydock) and they are rather of the race of the Marsi, who formerly claimed the same privilege, having made use of some drugs to prevent the poison. The ancients believed that they could charm serpents.
Blood. Jeremias xli. 6. Samson yielded to the tears of women, Judges xiv. 16., and xvi. 6.
Eyes. Is taken from ver. 16. It is not in Greek. (Haydock) — His tears are like those of crocodiles, which cry when they are going to kill a man. (Calmet)

Pride. We are naturally prone to it, and the friendship and manners of the proud will increase it. (Calmet) — If, therefore, the rich be not virtuous, it is dangerous to keep their company, (Worthington) both for this and the next world.
Kettle. Made of iron. It will presently be broken. So the poor must suffer, if they marry, or have society with those who are much above their rank. (Calmet)
Thou? Distrust those who promise much. (Calmet) — Spem pretio non emo. (Tertullian)
Drawn. Literally, “exhaust.” (Haydock) — He will feast thee, while he wants thy service, or he will come to dine with thee, and thus reduce thee to distress, Proverbs xxiii. 1. (Calmet)
Humbled. By foolishly attempting to rival the sumptuous feasts of the great. Ver. 9., and 11., are not in the Greek. (Haydock)

Wisdom. Depend not on others’ bounty. (Menochius) — When the cause of God is at stake, be firm, like St. Paul. (Calmet) — Pusillanimity in a superior might cause him to neglect his duty. (Worthington)
Concerning, &c., is not expressed in Greek. (Haydock) — If a person be so weak as to disclose his secret to a great man, he will never be trusted by him. (Calmet)
